The use of injections containing cells that are thought to have beneficial biologic properties (ie,
cell therapy) for the management of various musculoskeletal conditions (eg, osteoarthritis of
the knee) has expanded rapidly despite only low-level evidence to support its use.
The term stem cell therapy often is inappropriately used to describe, promote, and market
these therapies. The use of the term stem cell represents inappropriate and inaccurate hype
and should be strongly discouraged. Even if stem cells may be present in a population of cells
that are used for a given therapy, an assay of all cells in the population would reveal that a
true stem cell is the least abundant cell.
Concerns with regard to misinformation from direct-to-consumer marketing of unproven
treatment options have led to recent calls to action from professional organizations.

Current Cell Therapy Landscape
Musculoskeletal conditions are the leading cause of acute and chronic pain, physical
limitations in mobility, physician visits, and functional disability in the United States.1
Despite the large burden of disease, treatment options often are limited. In this state of
limited treatment options or failure with conventional therapies and in hope of avoiding
escalation in cost and risk, patients are vulnerable to unsubstantiated claims in direct-to-
consumer advertising of novel treatment options.2,3
Cellular therapies, and their theoretic potential to repair, augment, replace, or
regenerate diseased, damaged, or missing tissues has extraordinary intellectual and
emotional appeal. The concept of a stem cell and downstream progenitor populations
has been revolutionary in the past three decades of research in developmental biology,
genetics, and cancer. This fascination has been made even more powerful and
observable through the success of bone marrow transplantation; somatic nuclear
transfer and cloning; isolation of embryonic stem cells from mammalian and human
blastocysts; and, most recently, the recognition of nuclear reprograming and the
potential generation of patient-specific induced pluripotent stem cells, which was
awarded the Nobel Prize in 2011.4
Each tissue contains a population of stem and progenitor cells that is tissue-specific but
that may be plastic enough to be transplanted or induced (by a local biophysical,

chemical, and signaling environment) to differentiate into phenotypes not found in that
tissue (eg, bone formation in muscle or cartilage in synovium). The concentration,
prevalence, activation frequency, and expansion kinetics of these native stem and
progenitor populations are intrinsic variables that are intimately involved throughout life
in the control of normal growth and development; intrinsic response to injury, tissue
repair, and remodeling; and processes of tissue degeneration and postoperative healing
and recovery.
Every musculoskeletal connective tissue (eg, bone, cartilage, fat, muscle tendon,
ligament, synovium) contains a population of connective tissue stem cells and progenitor
cells. The term connective tissue progenitors (CTPs) has been defined to represent the
heterogeneous population of cells in native tissues that are capable of proliferating and
generating progeny that can differentiate into one or more connective tissues. This CTP
population represents the current opportunity for cell targeting harvest, processing, and
transplantation for cellular therapies. This heterogeneous CTP population also
represents the most valuable potential resource for purposeful cell selection and
targeted processing for generation of reproducible culture-expanded cell product in
vitro.
At a state of homeostasis in adult tissues, this population represents a continuum of
cells that are in constant transition at highly variable rates. Stem and progenitor cells
transition from upstream stem cells through a series of steps of activation, proliferation,
migration, and differentiation that later replaces mature cells lost to senescence or
disease. True stem cells reside in defined niches and divide rarely in an asymmetric
fashion to reproduce and preserve themselves for future cycles of cell division; however,
true stem cells are greatly outnumbered by progenitors that expand via cell division into
potentially thousands to millions of progenies. If the daughter of one stem cell division
divided at a mean of just 15 more times, it would generate more than 32,000 progeny,
and the ratio of stem cells to progenitors would be 1:32,000.5,6
Unfortunately, stem cells are rare and vastly outnumbered by progenitors. In addition,
progenitors also are rare, comprising only 1:1,000 to 1:1,000,000 cells in most connective
tissues.7-13 Culture expansion to increase the number of available cells is a logical
strategy. Unfortunately, in vitro expansion also exerts profound selection forces that
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:30 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002001
3/18

favor cells that attach and divide more quickly, and do not secrete auto-inhibitory
factors. These may not be the properties that are preferred. In addition, cells in culture
change constantly during expansion in vitro, and the changes that occur may not be
repeatable or reproducible. Culture-expanded cells age during expansion, losing their
potential for additional proliferation and usually also losing their potential to
differentiate, which often is considered to be their most desirable endpoints (ie, bone
and cartilage).
Unfortunately, the term stem cell has been attached to a broad range of cell-based
treatment strategies for various musculoskeletal conditions, especially knee
osteoarthritis. Aided by the excitement and hype of this provocative term, the demand
for these therapies has expanded rapidly. At the same time, the efficacy of these
therapies is supported by only low-level evidence14-16 (Resource 1). Most of these
therapies are marketed by clinicians who often have limited experience and training in
musculoskeletal care or in stem and progenitor cell biology, providing only so-called
stem cell treatments to all patients for various conditions and charging patients out-of-
pocket costs for such services17,18 (Resource 2). Public awareness of these so-called
stem cell or biologic therapies has been accelerated by their highly publicized use and
potentially incidental recovery in professional athletes.19 This environment has resulted
in inappropriate hype and misrepresentation of uncharacterized, minimally manipulated
cell preparations as stem cells, leading to widespread clinical use of unproven biologic
therapies.2,3
Concerns over misinformation from direct-to-consumer marketing of unproven
treatment options have led to recent calls to action from professional organizations,
including the National Academy of Sciences, the International Society for Cellular
Therapy, the American Association for the Advancement of Science, the Biologic
Association, and the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons.20-22 Each of these
organizations recognizes the potential value of cell therapies but is concerned about the
risk of exploitation that patients face in the current environment, the potential erosion of
public trust, and the responsible investment that will be necessary to bring legitimate
cellular and biologic therapies to patients.14

Stem Cell and Progenitor Cell Facts
Stem cells functioning in vivo in biologic systems have three general properties.
They are located in a specific niche, often in a specific anatomic location that is characterized
by specific supporting cells or extracellular matrix features.
They divide infrequently, generally remaining out of the cell cycle in G0 unless activated to
enter the cell cycle by local signaling.
They divide asymmetrically, giving rise to two daughter cells: one daughter cell remaining in
the stem cell niche (ie, resulting in self-renewal of the mother stem cell, preserving the stem
cell function for future cycles of activation) and a second daughter cell that leaves the stem
cell niche, going on to proliferate and generate a colony of progeny (ie, progenitors).
Progenitor cells functioning in vivo in biologic systems have three general properties.
After the formation of a progenitor in the initial asymmetric cell division of the upstream
stem cell, progenitors generally proliferate quickly for a period to generate a clone of
progeny that amplify the effect of each division of the founding stem cell.
The progenitor cells generally progress at the end of cell division to differentiate into one or
more differentiated cell phenotypes in response to intrinsic tissue-specific properties of the
stem cell niche from which they arise and the tissue-specific signaling environment in which
they expand and migrate.
Progenitor cells often can be expanded for many cell divisions without differentiating and
without loss of intrinsic biologic potential before committing to a differentiated phenotype.
This capacity for symmetric expansion, in which both daughter cells remain the same, has
been referred to as limited self-renewal. One progenitor, whose progeny continues to divide
for 16 cycles will generate 216 progeny, or more than 65,000 new cells.
During expansion, progenitor cell populations may pass through one or more transition
steps in which their biologic potential and anatomic location change, even before terminal
differentiation. Populations of progenitor cells that continue to expand during these
transition steps also have been referred to as transit expanding populations.
The cell division of the progenitor population, including transit expanding populations,
enables generation of appropriate numbers of mature differentiated cells for tissue
formation and remodeling and protects the upstream true stem cell from needing to divide
frequently to generate new cells. This reduces the risk of stem cell loss and the development
of genetic abnormalities from replication errors.
Stem cells and progenitor cells share some attributes.
They are capable of proliferation.

They are unspecialized but can give rise to progeny that will differentiate into specialized
cells.

Stem Cell and Progenitor Cell Facts
In any adult tissue, the number of progenitors will vastly outnumber the number of true
stem cells.
All tissue formation, repair, and remodeling require the formation of new cells.
Therefore, all tissue engineering, repair, and regeneration can only be accomplished via
the transplantation, activation, and proliferation of cells derived from upstream stem
cells or progenitor populations.
Almost all current cell therapies offered in the United States for musculoskeletal
conditions involve the harvest and transplantation of adult cells from tissues, often with
manipulation of some type designed to concentrate or select for stem or progenitor cell
populations. These tissues include blood, bone marrow, and fat. In the case of
musculoskeletal connective tissues (bone, cartilage, fat, muscle tendon, ligament,
synovium), every connective tissue contains a population of connective tissue stem cells
and progenitor cells;7-10 however, even after processing, they only constitute an
exceedingly small fraction of all the cells available in those tissue sources. Even in
processed cell populations, progenitors and true stem cells remain the least abundant
population in an otherwise heterogeneous population of tissue-derived cells. Therefore,
although transplantation of such cells may be considered to be cellular therapy (or cell
therapy), referring to the current populations of cells derived from blood, bone marrow,
or fat as stem cell therapies is inappropriate.
The concentration of stem and progenitor cells can be increased at the point of care via
density separation or other means to improve efficacy in some settings.23 Depending on
the tissue of origin, only 1 in 1,000 to 1 in 1 million cells harvested from healthy tissues
are stem or progenitor cells that are capable of differentiating into one or more
connective tissues, such as bone, cartilage, or fat.24-26 CTP cells have been defined as
the heterogenous population of tissue-resident cells that can be activated to proliferate

9/4/26, 10:30 AM
AAOS | Stem Cells and Cell Therapy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002001
6/18

and generate progeny that can be shown in vitro to differentiate into one or more
connective tissues.5,24-27
Stem and progenitor cells may be important in the mechanism of action of existing
cellular therapies; however, this is difficult to prove because their overall numbers are
low and because current evidence shows that current therapies result in new tissue
formation or long-term survival of the progeny of transplanted cells. For some
indications, more extensive manipulation or in vitro culture expansion may be necessary
to select for, isolate, and/or adequately enrich for optimal stem or progenitor cells for a
given application; however, at this time, the primary mechanism of action of current
cellular therapies must be assumed to derive from the effect of soluble factors,
microvesicles, or signaling molecules that are embedded in the extracellular matrix that
is elaborated by transplanted cells, many of which may be neither a progenitor nor a
stem cell.
A large quantity of literature uses the terminology of culture-expanded cells from bone
marrow or other tissue commonly referred to as mesenchymal stem cells or
mesenchymal stromal cells (both abbreviated as MSCs), adding to the confusion
regarding stem cells.20,28,29 To improve clarity in communication and accuracy in
nomenclature, the International Society for Cellular Therapy adopted a definition for
MSCs that purposefully dropped the use of the term stem and defined MSCs to be
mesenchymal stromal cells. They also defined specific attributes that were required for
designation of a cell population as MSCs: adherence to tissue culture plastic; absence of
hematopoietic cell markers (eg, cluster of differentiation (CD) 4, CD8, CD19, CD31, CD34);
expression of surface markers considered to be characteristic of culture-expanded MSCs
(CD73, CD90, and CD105); and evidence that the cells can differentiate into and express
markers of osteoblasts, adipocytes, and chondrocytes in vitro under appropriate media
conditions.20 To date, decades of in vitro and animal research have explored the
potential for culture-expanded MSCs to form new tissue after transplantation; however,
clinical translation has largely failed. Evidence shows that some culture-expanded MSC
populations will secrete immunomodulatory factors that may improve the environment
of tissue repair or clinical symptoms. Evidence shows that infusion of some MSC
populations may mitigate clinical graft versus host disease; however, at this time, MSC

therapies have not yet been cleared by the US FDA for human clinical application to
musculoskeletal diseases.
Cell Therapy Facts
Clinical therapies that involve the transplantation of viable nucleated cells as presumed
therapeutic agents can be appropriately defined as cellular therapy or cell therapy.
Clinical therapies that preferentially exclude nucleated cells from the preferred mixture of
components (eg, leukocyte poor/platelet-rich plasma, platelet-poor plasma, exosomes, tissue
matrix extracts) should not be referred to as cellular therapies.
Cell populations or preparations that are intended for use as therapies should be
characterized and defined with respect to the concentration and prevalence of the various cell
types in the population. Untested and uncharacterized cell therapy formulations need to be
clearly understood by practitioners and clearly communicated within the profession, to
patients, and to the public.

Cell Therapy Facts
The efficacy of cell therapies is assumed to be dependent on cell source (donor, systemic
health and local donor tissue health), recipient (systemic health, usually the same as the
donor), local tissue environment (vascularity, scar, mechanical environment), and the
concentration and prevalence of the various cell populations in the therapy. The
composition of cells will depend on the harvest technique and the processing technique
that are used and on the conditions used for expansion (if used).
Overall, the consensus is that the term stem cell has been overused as a marketing term
to promote cellular therapies that consists of uncharacterized populations of minimally
manipulated autogenous or even allograft cells and tissue-derived culture-expanded cell
populations.9,20 The use of the term stem cell to describe minimally manipulated cell
preparations is problematic and has created substantial confusion for patients,
physicians, and the general public. This has prompted a recommendation that the use of
minimally manipulated cell products and tissue-derived culture-expanded cells be

referred to as cell therapy and that the untested and uncharacterized nature of these
treatment options be clearly communicated within the profession, to patients, and to the
public14,30 (Resource 3).
Engineering Principles of Clinical Cell-Based Tissue Engineering
Four major cell-based tissue-engineering strategies exist.
Targeting local cells, including stem and progenitor cells if new tissue is desired
Transplanting cells, including autogenous stem and progenitor cells
Transplanting culture-expanded or modified stem and progenitor cells
Transplanting cells in fully formed tissue constructs generated in vitro or in vivo

Engineering Principles of Clinical Cell-Based Tissue Engineering
Four major cell-based tissue-engineering strategies exist: targeting local cells, including
stem and progenitor cells if new tissue is desired; transplanting cells, including
autogenous stem and progenitor cells; transplanting culture-expanded or modified stem
and progenitor cells; and transplanting cells in fully formed tissue generated in vitro or in
vivo (Resource 4). Stem cell function is controlled by changes in stem cell activation and
self-renewal or by changes in the proliferation, migration, differentiation, or survival of
the progeny generated after each stem cell activation. Three-dimensional porous
scaffolds promote new tissue formation by providing a surface and void volume that
aids the attachment, migration, proliferation, and desired differentiation of CTPs
throughout the region in which new tissue is needed. Critical variables in scaffold design
and function include the bulk material or materials from which it is made; the three-
dimensional architecture; the surface chemistry; the mechanical properties; the initial
chemical environment around the scaffold; and the late scaffold chemical environment,
which is often determined by degradation characteristics. Local presentation or delivery
of bioactive molecules can change the function of CTPs (ie, activation, proliferation,
migration, differentiation, or survival) in a manner that results in new or enhanced local
tissue formation. All cells require access to substrate molecules (eg, oxygen, glucose, and
amino acids). These substrates may be made available to cells via diffusion through the
extracellular matrix around each cell. However, diffusion is slow, and highly cellular

9/18

tissues can only be supported by mass transport via convection through vascular
perfusion in which every cell is less than a fraction of a millimeter away from a perfused
capillary bed. Transplanted cells are particularly vulnerable. A balance between
consumption and local delivery of these substrates must be maintained if transplanted
cells are to survive. Theoretic calculations can be used to explore the relationships
among cell density, diffusion distance, and cell viability within a graft and to design
improved strategies for transplantation of CTPs. Rational strategies for tissue
engineering seek to optimize new tissue formation through the logical selection of
conditions that modulate the performance of CTPs in a graft site to produce a desired
tissue. This increasingly involves strategies that combine matrices, inductive stimuli, and
techniques that enhance the survival and performance of local or transplanted CTPs.26
In particular, cell survival depends not on transplanting increasing numbers of cells but
on selecting and transplanting lower numbers of more specifically selected cells, with
fewer local competitors for limited substrates.
Clinical Evidence for Cell-Based Therapies in Orthopaedic Surgery
Cell-based therapies for the management of musculoskeletal conditions are at considerable
risk for bias, and evidence-based recommendations for their use in clinical practice currently is
limited.
Standardization with respect to the quantitative and qualitative characterization of methods
for cell harvest, cell processing, and cell transplantation/delivery are lacking in the reported
clinical literature.

Clinical Evidence for Cell-Based Therapies in Orthopaedic Surgery
Recently, interest in cell-based therapies in orthopaedics as adjuncts or alternatives to
surgical management has increased.31 The exponential increase in interest has been
reflected by the global cellular therapy market, which is projected to attain a market
valuation of $14.8 billion US dollars by 2022.32 The use of cell-based interventions has
anecdotally spanned a plethora of orthopaedic and non-orthopaedic interventions;14

AAOS | Stem Cells and Cell Therapy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002001
10/18

however, evidence-based implementation of proven cell-based therapeutics within
orthopaedic surgery is limited to a number of formulations and specific musculoskeletal
disorders, most importantly osteoarthritis, osteonecrosis, and tendinopathies.14,33
Osteoarthritis, particularly of the knee, constitutes the most extensive application of
proven and often unproven cell-based therapies in orthopaedic surgery. Given the
considerable controversy regarding supporting evidence, Chahla et al34 conducted a
systematic review of six level II and III studies to analyze the efficacy of using adipose
tissue, bone marrow, or blood-derived cells with or without platelet-rich plasma and high
tibial osteotomy/microfracture in patients with knee osteoarthritis. The authors reported
that, although the addition of cell-based therapeutics conferred more remarkable
postoperative improvement in patient-reported outcomes, such improvement was
modest, and a placebo effect cannot be disregarded. In a more recent review, Ha et al35
corroborated the aforementioned findings via an analysis of 17 studies, including six
randomized controlled trials on the effect of intra-articular MSC injection (eg, bone
marrow, adipose, umbilical cord, and stromal vascular fraction-derived stem cells) with
and without surgical management on clinical outcomes and cartilage repair in patients
with knee osteoarthritis. Fifteen of the included studies corroborated greater
improvement in visual analog scale pain scale scores, walking time, the number of stairs,
Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index scores, Medical
Outcomes Study 12-Item and 26-Item Short Form scores, Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis
Outcome scores, International Knee Documentation Committee scores, Hospital for
Special Surgery scores, and Tegner activity scores among recipients of cellular
therapeutics. Overall, evidence indicates potential benefits in using cell-based
therapeutics in the management of early-stage osteoarthritis. Cell therapy has been
found to be symptom-modifying; however, little evidence currently suggests that these
treatment options are structure-modifying. Additional studies, particularly with level I
evidence, are required to better understand the role of adjunctive cell therapy in
patients with knee osteoarthritis.
Cell-based therapies have been extensively used as adjuncts to core decompression
procedures for osteonecrosis of the femoral head.14,31,36 Studies indicate that
combined core decompression and intralesional administration of cellular therapeutics
may prolong native hip survivorship and, subsequently, time to conversion to total hip

arthroplasty. Piuzzi et al25,37 performed a systematic review on the use of cell therapies
for the management of osteonecrosis of the femoral head. The authors concluded that
these therapies were safe and reported improved clinical outcomes with lower disease
progression rate. Specifically, all 10 studies that reported patient-reported outcomes
showed improved outcomes in the cell therapy groups compared with the control
groups (core decompression alone). Overall, radiographic progression was observed in
24.5% (93 of 380) of the hips that received cell therapy compared with 40% (98 of 245) of
the hips in the control group. Nine of 10 studies that reported failure rates showed a
lower rate of conversion to total hip arthroplasty in the cell therapy group (16%; 62/380
hips) compared with the control group (21%; 52/252 hips).25,37 Hernigou et al38
prospectively compared long-term survivorship (20 to 30 years) among 125 hips with
pre-collapse osteonecrosis that were managed via core decompression with or without
the administration of bone marrow–derived cells (BMDCs). The authors determined that
at a mean follow-up of 25 years, survivorship of the native hip was 76% in the BMDC
cohort versus 24% in the core decompression–only cohort. Kang et al corroborated
these findings in 106 hips with pre-collapse and post-collapse disease, reporting 71.7%
survivorship in hips treated via BMDC and core decompression versus 51% survivorship
in hips treated via core decompression only at a mean follow-up of 4.28 years.39 In a
recent systematic review, Mont et al36 analyzed studies published between 2015 and
2019 on the influence of cellular therapies (eg, platelet-rich plasma, bone marrow cells,
bone marrow aspirate concentrate, human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells, and
fibroblast growth factor-2) in combination with core decompression on native hip
survivorship in hips with osteonecrosis of the femoral head. Of the six comparative
studies included, four studies reported marked improvement in survivorship with core
decompression and cellular therapies versus core decompression alone. Similar to that
reported across different conditions, standardization with respect to the quantitative
and qualitative characterization of methods for cell harvest, cell processing, and cell
transplantation/delivery is lacking in the osteonecrosis literature.25
Tendinopathies are among the most prevalent disorders, with an incidence that may
surpass 50% among certain athletic populations.40 Despite the abundant treatment
options, which include surgical and nonsurgical options, outcomes often are
unsatisfactory,41 which engenders a drive to explore alternative interventions,
particularly those that are minimally invasive or nonsurgical treatment options. Although

contemporary literature describes clinical outcomes for cell-based therapeutic
interventions in lateral epicondylar, patellar, Achilles, and rotator cuff tendinopathies,
comparative studies have only analyzed the latter two applications.42 Hernigou et al43
evaluated the efficacy of isolated arthroscopic surgical repair versus combined repair
and local injection of BMDC in 90 patients with rotator cuff tears. The authors assessed
patients for evidence of healing via MRI/ultrasonography and for any incidence of re-tear
for a follow-up as long as 10 years. The authors reported that the use of BMDC as an
adjunctive therapy during rotator cuff repair enhanced the healing rate and improved
the quality of the repaired tendon as determined by ultrasonography and MRI. By 6
months postoperatively, healing was observed in 45 of 45 rotator cuffs in the BMDC
cohort compared with 30 of 45 (67%) rotator cuffs in the repair-only cohort. In addition,
at a follow-up of 10 years, 39 of 45 (87%) intact rotator cuff repairs were reported in the
BMDC cohort compared to 20 of 45 (44%) intact rotator cuff repairs in the repair-only
cohort. The authors highlighted that the number of transplanted cells was the most
important factor influencing outcomes, which was evidenced by patients who received
fewer BMDCs having the highest incidence of tendon re-rupture during the 10-year
follow-up interval. Regardless, this study and the currently available evidence are of the
level III tier. A recent systematic review by Van den Boom et al42 reported that only level
III evidence is available to support the efficacy of cell-based therapy for tendon
disorders. Therefore, findings are at considerable risk for bias, and evidence-based
recommendations for the use of cell-based therapy for tendon disorders in clinical
practice cannot be made at this time.
